task_row_model.query: In a hemodynamically stable adult with suspected acute pulmonary embolism but severe renal impairment (eGFR <30 mL/min) that contraindicates CT pulmonary angiography with iodinated contrast, what is the recommended diagnostic algorithm and initial anticoagulation strategy? Please include the roles of D-dimer, V/Q scanning, point-of-care ultrasound (leg duplex and echocardiography), and the choice between unfractionated heparin, LMWH, DOACs, or warfarin.

documents.content: Ventilation–perfusion (V/Q) scintigraphy remains a key alternative to CT pulmonary angiography when iodinated contrast is contraindicated. A normal chest radiograph increases the diagnostic yield of V/Q; a normal V/Q scan effectively excludes clinically significant pulmonary embolism. Mismatched perfusion defects in one or more lobes are suggestive of PE, but nondiagnostic or low-probability V/Q scans require further testing. V/Q is less useful when the chest radiograph shows significant parenchymal disease, and interpretation should be correlated with pretest probability and clinical features.

documents.content: Pulmonary embolism diagnosis and management during pregnancy prioritizes maternal and fetal safety. Because ionizing radiation and contrast exposure carry specific risks, ventilation–perfusion scanning is often preferred when feasible; if CT pulmonary angiography is required, shielding and low-dose protocols are used. Anticoagulation typically uses low molecular weight heparin throughout pregnancy with attention to dosing and anti-Xa monitoring in extremes of weight. Thrombolysis and invasive interventions are reserved for life-threatening events. Multidisciplinary discussion with obstetrics is essential for delivery planning and postpartum anticoagulation.

documents.content: For a hemodynamically stable patient with suspected PE and severe renal impairment, begin with clinical pretest probability (Wells or gestalt). In low or moderate probability, D-dimer testing may be used but has reduced specificity in renal failure; a negative result can help rule out PE. If imaging is needed, a V/Q scan is preferred when the chest radiograph is not abnormal; a normal V/Q excludes PE. If V/Q is nondiagnostic, perform bilateral lower-extremity duplex ultrasound to detect DVT, and use focused echocardiography to assess right ventricular strain if available. If clinical probability is high, start empirical anticoagulation unless bleeding risk contraindicates it. For eGFR <30 mL/min, unfractionated heparin is preferred because it is easily titratable and reversible; LMWH requires dose adjustment and anti-Xa monitoring and is used cautiously. DOACs are generally avoided in severe renal impairment per labeling; transition to warfarin with overlap or monitored UFH can be considered for long-term therapy. Consider IVC filter only if anticoagulation is absolutely contraindicated.

documents.content: Anticoagulation choices in patients with reduced renal function require careful agent selection and monitoring. Unfractionated heparin is preferred in severe renal impairment because of nonrenal clearance, a short half-life, and rapid reversibility with protamine. Low molecular weight heparins have renal clearance and require dose reduction or anti-Xa monitoring when eGFR is low; accumulation increases bleeding risk. Direct oral anticoagulants are variably renally excreted and many are contraindicated or require dose adjustments below an eGFR threshold; consult specific drug labels. Warfarin remains an option for long-term therapy with bridging until INR is therapeutic.

documents.content: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) is a long-term consequence of unresolved pulmonary emboli leading to pulmonary vascular obstruction and progressive right heart failure. Diagnosis relies on persistent perfusion defects on V/Q scanning after at least three months of therapeutic anticoagulation, plus confirmation with right heart catheterization showing elevated pulmonary vascular resistance. Management includes lifelong anticoagulation, consideration of pulmonary thromboendarterectomy for surgically accessible disease, and pulmonary vasodilator therapy or balloon pulmonary angioplasty for inoperable cases. Early referral to a specialized center is recommended.
